title: What can you say about ginger in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 2 wordings for ginger; the strongest is "Helps reduce nausea and vomiting from motion sickness or seasickness" (moderate, 0.5-3 g dried rhizome (or extract equivalent) a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Relieves bronchitis, coughs and colds".

supported_wordings.wording: Helps reduce nausea and vomiting from motion sickness or seasickness.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it as a non-traditional use with travel directions; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: 0.5-3 g dried rhizome (or extract equivalent) a day
supported_wordings.dose_details: Children 6-11, adolescents and adults. Take one dose 30 minutes before travel, then every 4 hours as needed. Aqueous extracts: 0.7-3 g.

supported_wordings.wording: Traditionally used in herbal medicine to help relieve occasional digestive upset, such as indigestion, nausea, gas or lack of appetite.
supported_wordings.why: Traditional use in Health Canada's monograph; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: 0.3-3 g dried rhizome (or extract equivalent) a day
supported_wordings.dose_details: Children 6-11, adolescents and adults. Aqueous extracts: 0.7-3 g.

wordings_to_avoid.why: Names a disease; no listed source supports it.
FDA's 2000 rule (page 1029) gives 'reduces nausea associated with chemotherapy' as a disease claim.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

sources.name: FDA final rule on structure/function statements, 65 FR 1000 (6 January 2000), page 1031 (the OTC antiemetic monograph's motion-sickness claim)

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
